prize_parts.citation: for the invention and experimental realization of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength open a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single-part prize for B049, Katori and Ye. It meets the test I apply in this committee. There is an original idea (the magic-wavelength lattice, which cancels the light shift while holding many atoms Doppler- and recoil-free), a realization in a working instrument, and independent verification by several laboratories with clocks compared across continents. It is a tool that opens a door: fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, centimetre-scale relativistic geodesy, constraints on variation of constants, and a basis for redefining the second. The round-1 exchange strengthened my view that the quality of the evidence is not in dispute; the chair's summary records that no member challenges the experimental maturity of B049, and six of eight members name it. I do not treat that count as the argument. The argument is that the lattice clock is the only shortlisted candidate where every element I require (original idea, realized instrument, replication, concrete new measurements) can be checked against the record, and the credit can be stated in two names.
statement.case_against: The serious objections are about credit and overlap, not about whether the result is real. First, the discovery-versus-instrument question: a clock is a measurement capability, and no departure from expectation (drifting constants, a dark-matter signal) has yet appeared. I accept that this is a legitimate reservation, but the committee has honoured the invention of enabling instruments and methods before, provided the new regime they open is demonstrated rather than promised, and here it has been demonstrated in geodesy-scale redshift measurements and in many-body clock physics. Second, the 2005 and 2012 prizes: the citation must be anchored to the many-atom magic-wavelength scheme and not to precision spectroscopy in general, so that the boundary against the frequency comb and ion-control prizes is explicit. Third, Ye's share. I still hold that the original idea and first realization are Katori's, and I keep two names only if the citation and record state that the realization includes taking the scheme to its accuracy limit and showing that density-dependent effects can be controlled. Contributions by Lemonde, Gill, Takamoto, Lisdat and Ludlow remain outside the two names and the public explanation must say so.

responses.point: Lindroth calls the two-name credit compact and attributable, and says the lattice clock is a conceptual step beyond 2005 and 2012, while acknowledging that Ye's contribution is partly performance and refinement and that she has not checked priority against the primary papers.
responses.response: In round 1 I asked whether the prize would stand with Katori alone, and I have now reasoned it through. It would stand scientifically, because the concept is his. But the experimental discovery I am asked to verify is that the scheme actually delivers: that lattice light shifts and atomic collisions can be controlled to the 1e-18 level in a many-atom ensemble. A prize that credited only the proposal and the first demonstration would leave out the work that made it a result others reproduced, and the many-body clock measurements are the physics that goes beyond the earlier instruments. I therefore keep Ye alongside Katori, but on the stated ground that the realization includes the demonstration of control, not that precision alone earns a prize. I share your caution that priority has to be checked against primary papers, and I rely on the citation wording to make this explicit.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B049 first on the strength of the measured number being reproduced by other groups, but notes that part of the scientific harvest (redefinition of the second, geodesy at scale, constants tests) is still prospective and that Ye's comb and spectroscopy work is intertwined with the clock work.
responses.response: I agree that the reproducibility of the number is the decisive evidence, and it is the kind of evidence an experimentalist trusts. On the prospective harvest I draw a different line than you do. The prize criteria require experimental verification of the discovery, not completion of every application. Centimetre-scale height differences resolved with clocks, and comparisons across continents that agree to this level, are already delivered measurements, not promises. The redefinition of the second is a consequence we need not wait for, and I would not tie the citation to it. I do accept your point on intertwining: the citation should name the lattice clock, not Ye's frequency-comb or molecule work, so that we credit one achievement and not a career.

responses.point: Pearce proposes a two-part prize, B049 plus B047 (Halzen alone), keeping the second part as droppable, and discloses field affinity for IceCube.
responses.response: I respect the chair's wish to recognise a new observational window, and I said in round 1 that I do not oppose B047 on merit. After the exchange my position is that I cannot support it as a second part. The whole committee has now said the single name cannot be defended from the supplied material, and you concede this yourself. A second part with a credit that we cannot verify weakens the prize and, more importantly, exposes us to crediting a leader and not the people who did the original work. The same standard rules out my own earlier preference, the quantum cascade laser, which I dropped when the evidence for the clock was stronger. I would not oppose a two-part prize in principle, but I will not vote for one just to add a second area when the attribution of that part is open.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B024 (Luk, Kim, Wang) as a clean discovery from nature that unlocked CP-violation searches, and says the overlap with the 2015 prize and Double Chooz and accelerator appearance results are the open points.
responses.response: I accept that theta-13 is a real discovery with no maturity problem, and I take seriously your own admission that its breadth of support is the thinnest of your candidates. My difficulty in round 1 was that I could not verify the historical record behind the credited trio, and that has not changed: the near-simultaneous Daya Bay, RENO and Double Chooz announcements, and the T2K and MINOS appearance data, make the three-name set harder to defend than a two-person clock credit. You have not stated which of the overlap and credit points you treat as decisive, and until the committee can say who did the original experiment I keep B024 outside my configuration. If the committee does not carry B049, it is a fallback I would consider, though not ahead of B048.

responses.point: Eriksson alone prefers B048 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as a compound theory-plus-HgTe citation, citing fifteen years of independent confirmation, and admits he cannot say how well edge-conductance quantisation has been reproduced outside the Molenkamp group.
responses.response: As someone who looks at interfaces and heterostructures, I find the HgTe quantum-well experiment convincing as an original experiment, and the Z2 distinction from the 2016 prize is clear. Your own caution about imperfect edge-channel quantisation is the point that matters to me: the experiment is decisive for existence rather than for ideal protection, and the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang from a prize whose experiment rests on their prediction is a credit problem that three names cannot fix. For that reason it is my first alternative, not my preferred configuration. If the committee rejected B049, B048 is where I would turn next, with a citation confined to the quantum spin Hall effect.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as a discovery-class achievement or as an instrument and metrology advance; I think the delivered measurements (geodesy, comparisons) decide it, but no departure from expectation has yet been measured.
Whether Katori alone would be the more defensible attribution; I keep two names but regard Ye's share as resting on the realization and control of the scheme, not on the original idea.

The exact boundary against the 2005 (frequency comb) and 2012 (ion control) prizes and against other lattice-clock groups; this depends on the citation wording, which I cannot check against primary papers here.
Priority details come from memory and the supplied credit, not from verified records, and I may misstate who first realized specific steps.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any candidate in my configuration or alternatives. Goran Johansson is a Chalmers Physics colleague and flagged his own bias on circuit QED and trapped ions, which are outside my configuration; Mehlig and I are also colleagues without joint work. My field (electron microscopy) has no direct link to lattice clocks, the IceCube, topological insulator or diamond NV candidates. I request no recusal, and my position has not changed since round 1 on this point.
